titles.A1: Need Private Grad Loans? Variable vs Fixed Through History
titles.B1: Why a Variable Loan Can Rise Above Fixed and Still Cost Less
titles.D: 7.5% Variable or 9% Fixed? Grad Loans Through History
titles.X: Fixed vs Variable Student Loans Explained

loglines.A: Since July 1, 2026, new graduate students can no longer get federal Grad PLUS loans, and the federal loan they can still get stops at a yearly limit. Students who need more turn to private lenders, who usually offer two kinds of rate: a variable rate that can start lower, or a fixed rate that never changes. This video takes one illustrative $50,000, 10-year private loan — 7.5% variable against 9% fixed — and replays it through every 10-year stretch of US interest rates since 1954, to show how often the lower start ended up costing more in total, how bad the worst stretch was, and how the answer changes when the head start is bigger, smaller, or zero. History, not a forecast.
loglines.B: Take a variable-rate grad loan that starts at 7.5% and replay it through every 10-year stretch of US interest rates since 1954. In about three of every four stretches, its rate climbed above a 9% fixed rate at some point. Yet over the whole loan it cost more far less often — in more than one in four stretches that began before 1981, and about one in thirty after. This video follows one illustrative $50,000, 10-year loan through both kinds of history, including the worst stretch, which began in April 1977, to show how both facts can be true. History, not a forecast.
loglines.W: A backtest of 753 overlapping 120-month windows of the 3-month Treasury bill rate (TB3MS, start months 1954–2016) computes the distribution of total-interest differences between a 7.5% variable-rate and a 9% fixed-rate amortizing loan, and reports the share of windows in which the variable loan costs more, the median difference and the maximum difference.
